Where it began

Michael Holding was born in Kingston, Jamaica, on 16 February 1954. He grew up the youngest of four in a sporting family, and his father signed him up at Melbourne Cricket Club in Kingston when he was very small. The family often went to watch at Sabina Park, but young Michael was always keener to be playing than looking on.

He would go on to play first-class cricket for Jamaica, and in England and beyond for Canterbury, Derbyshire, Lancashire and Tasmania.

The player

He made his Test debut on the 1975 tour of Australia and quickly became Andy Roberts's natural partner with the new ball. In 1976, at The Oval, he took eight for 92 and 14 wickets in the match, which set a West Indies record for a Test match. In all he played 60 Tests from 1975 to 1987 and took 249 wickets at 23.69, with 13 five-wicket innings.

He was a key part of the side that won the 1979 World Cup, where nobody in his side took more wickets. In 33 Tests opening together, he and Roberts took 216 wickets, and they were at the heart of the great West Indian pace attacks of the late seventies and early eighties.

What made him special

Standing 6 ft 4 in, he ran in so smoothly and quietly that he earned the nickname Whispering Death. The action was smooth, the pace was frightening and the bounce was steep. In Bridgetown in 1981 he bowled an over to Geoff Boycott that is often called the greatest in Test history: five balls each a little quicker than the last, then one that knocked back the stumps to roars from the crowd.

Batting was more of a hobby. He never made a Test hundred, but six fifties show he could swing the bat, and in 1984 he and Viv Richards put on an unbeaten 106 for the last wicket in a one-day international, a record at the time.

Away from the middle

He won a scholarship to study computer science at the University of the West Indies, and later ran a petrol station in Kingston. A friend at Radio Jamaica talked him into commentary, and in 1990 he moved to television alongside Tony Cozier. His calm, deep voice became familiar around the cricket world until he stepped away from the microphone in September 2021.

He wrote books including Whispering Death, in 1988, and No Holding Back, in 2010. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year, he joined the ICC Hall of Fame and in 2013 he received an honorary degree from the University of East London.

And finally

In 1988 Jamaica put him on a two-dollar stamp. When the ICC invited him onto its cricket committee in 2007, he thought at first that one of his friends was having him on.
